summary: Adds the LoST-Validation service tag to the S-NAPTR Application Service Tag IANA registry. The tag can appear in a NAPTR DNS record to help clients of the Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) protocol find servers designated for location validation, and it updates RFC 5222. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: Special labels in an internet phonebook can show what a server does. This document adds one label so programs can find the servers that check whether an address is valid.

subtitle: A new DNS service tag that lets emergency-location software find the servers that check addresses, separate from the ones that route calls.

tldr.problem: LoST servers can map a location to a service and also validate civic addresses, but clients had no explicit way to find servers designated for validation, which some deployments keep separate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers a 'LoST-Validation' S-NAPTR application service tag. Clients resolving a validation server try this tag first and fall back to the 'LoST' tag.
tldr.outcome: Deployments can split mapping and validation across server clusters without relying on DNS naming conventions. The RFC updates RFC 5222 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8917 is a Proposed Standard, published in October 2020, and it updates RFC 5222. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Scope of the Document
sections.content:
RFC 8917 adds the LoST-Validation tag to the S-NAPTR Application Service Tag IANA registry. The tag is used in Naming Authority Pointer (NAPTR) DNS records so that clients of the Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) protocol can identify servers designated for location validation.

The tag and the information on its use are an update to RFC 5222, enabling the explicit discovery of a server that supports location validation.
sections.plainLanguage: It adds one new label to the phonebook so programs can find the helpers that check whether an address is real.

sections.title: Why Mapping and Validation Are Separated
sections.content:
LoST defines a mapping service and also lets a client ask that a civic address be validated. Servers are allowed to ignore a validation request. The National Emergency Number Association (NENA) defines an all-IP emergency services architecture called i3, which treats mapping and validation as two distinct functions: the Emergency Call Routing Function (ECRF) and the Location Validation Function (LVF). i3 requires that they be separable.

The rationale is that mapping is used in real time during emergency call routing, while validation is used in advance, typically when data is provisioned. Mapping therefore has much higher availability and response-time requirements. An organization might use separate clusters to shield mapping from bursty validation load, or one cluster for both.

Because LoST referrals return an Application Unique String (AUS) rather than a URL, a different service tag or a DNS name convention is needed to tell the services apart. DNS name conventions are inflexible and fragile, so a separate tag is preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: One helper needs to answer urgent calls instantly, and another checks addresses ahead of time. A busy checking day should not slow the urgent helper, so they may be different teams.

sections.title: How the LoST-Validation Tag Is Used
sections.content:
The LoST-Validation tag is a counterpart to the LoST tag added by RFC 5222. LoST identifies servers for the core mapping function, and LoST-Validation identifies servers designated for validation. NAPTR records for such servers contain the new tag.

A client needing validation follows the discovery procedure in RFC 5222, except that it uses the LoST-Validation tag in preference to LoST. Both tags use the HTTP and HTTPS URL schemes. If no NAPTR records carry the new tag, the LoST tag is used, and fallback to LoST may also follow if the new tag does not give a usable server.

The two tags might resolve to the same URL or to different URLs, and different URLs could lead to the same physical servers or to different ones.
sections.plainLanguage: To find a checking helper, first look for the 'checker' label. If there is none, use the general label instead, because that helper might do the checking too.

sections.title: Backwards Compatibility
sections.content:
Within North America, the NENA i3 document specifies how protocols such as LoST are used, and it is expected to reference the new tag. A client written before the tag existed uses the LoST tag. If it asks a designated mapping server for validation, the server may perform it, or return the locationValidationUnavailable warning, possibly with a redirect element holding a different AUS that resolves to a validation server.

In the worst case the client cannot reach a server willing to validate and follows up, for example by submitting a discrepancy report as specified in NENA i3. The RFC notes this situation can exist with or without the new tag, and that using the tag improves the likelihood that a client can validate a location when needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Old programs keep working. They might just be told 'ask someone else' or 'try later' more often than programs that know the new label.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3958, RFC 4848 and RFC 5222 apply, and no additional security aspects are foreseen from adding one more tag. Separation may be wanted to give the mapping and validation services different levels of resources such as capacity, attack mitigation and bandwidth, which requires separate tags.

Since DNS security has become more widely deployed since RFC 5222, such measures SHOULD be used when performing NAPTR resolution. There can be valid reasons to proceed with a mapping query despite security failures during an emergency call, but these generally do not apply to a validation query done in advance.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding one more label does not make things less safe. The usual protections for the phonebook should still be used, especially when checking addresses ahead of time.

sections.title: The IANA Registration
sections.content:
IANA added LoST-Validation to the S-NAPTR Application Service Tags registry created by RFC 3958. The registration lists the Application Service Tag as LoST-Validation and the Defining Publication as this document.

The RFC notes that IANA and RFC 3958 call the registry S-NAPTR Application Service Tags, while RFC 5222 calls it the U-NAPTR application service tag registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of labels now includes the new one, with this document named as the place that explains it.
